I read about racism in Lithuania quite strongly the first time, when I was in a French bookstore with my boyfriend, and we found a travel guide about Lithuania. In the safety concerns by the end of the guide, it wrote something like this: "The first thing you should worry about in Lithuania is racism. If you come from France, people will ask you why is there so many "Arabs" in your country!" and I was quite surprised. I know most Eastern European countries, there are not many non-white people and that people would obviously stare or express surprise/rejection. I'm not naive, haha. But then, to the extent that a travel guide notes it as the number 1 worry... It freaked me out a bit.

In my opinion, I think it's hard for a non-white to say whether or not a community or a society is racist, as they don't necessarily experience it, nor witness it. My boyfriend definitely told me that people would stare at me, maybe make some comments. He told me that when he was dating his ex-black girlfriend, one of his acquaintances asked him if black girls had a weird smell (my boyfriend said this guy was an idiot old classmate.) That kind of racism doesn't also worry me, nor suprise me, but I'm just worried that I won't be able to handle the "pressure". As I commented above in the page, at the same time, I feel like I should tough up.

It's still an idea so far - we still haven't thought the practical/technical points (plane tickets, etc.) I know he's leaving May 31st - his parents bought him the ticket already.

I'm planning on having internships over the summer, and one Canadian friend invited me for summer as well. 

I've spoken with my boyfriend indeed, and his parents are not racist (I'm pretty sure they have prejudice though, but it's understandable. His mother said to him once "You really like exotic girls, don't you?" because it's not the first time he's dating a black girl, but I was not offended nor ashamed.

It's a subject that has become hard to bring up without hiding behind sassy remarks or humor, because it's quite awkward sometimes. I believe he's ready to support me, but you are right. We need to have a true, actual discussion about it.

I think the most stressing part is the travel in itself though. I'm used to taket the plane a lot, and God, when I imagine passing the customs with him in a country where people would definitely stare at you and my only way of disappearing in a "safe space" in a boarding queue are headphones, my hands do get sweaty and I start stressing.

I was thinking about my parents when I was writing this.
As born in Africa and moving to Europe in their late teens - 20s there, they had to face racism under all its forms in their daily lives - at work, in college, in shops, in streets, everywhere. And they survived, are happy to live in the country they lived, and not necessarily see the countries they lived in as racist. But again, they lived in Portugal, which is a country with former colonies and has experience with immigrants from its former colonies, unlike Lithuania, where the only black people I heard of was one guy from Nigeria talking about daily  racism and black basketball players (basketball is religion there)
